manifest.name: dsh-agent-relay-plugin
manifest.description: DSH plugin: durable messaging between native agent sessions — DSH sessions and Codex threads, push in both directions, with thread discovery and session creation.
manifest.author: Lyuwen Fu <fulvwen@gmail.com>

scripts.build: rm -rf dist && tsc -p tsconfig.json && node tools/build-runtime.mjs
scripts.check: npm run typecheck && node --check src/core.mjs && node --check src/bridge.mjs && node --check src/codex.mjs && node --check src/mcp.mjs

bundle.text:
# Agent Relay bundle patch layer.
#
# This bundle inserts one Host row and leaves it disabled, so installing the
# package changes nothing until an operator enables it in a profile user layer
# (`$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`). Enable it with, for example:
#
#   - id: agent-relay
#     disabled: false
#     config:
#       codexProxy: /home/you/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock
#       codexExecutable: /usr/local/bin/codex
#       allowSessionCreation: true
#       externalMembers:
#         - id: codex-tui
#           tokenFile: /home/you/.dsh/agent-relay/codex-tui.token
#
# Layer order (DSH docs): bundle layers in profile order, then the profile's
# cordis.patch.yml, then $DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml, then --patch overlays.
# A later layer replaces a row's whole `config`, so repeat every key you need.
#
# Defaults filled in by the plugin: teamId=relay, bridgePort=33120, journal at
# $DSH_HOME/agent-relay/journal.jsonl (status/log beside it), and attachment to
# the default Codex daemon socket when no transport is configured.
- insert:
    - id: agent-relay
      name: dsh-agent-relay-plugin
      disabled: true
      config:
        teamId: relay

readme.text:
Durable, bidirectional messaging between native agent sessions, shipped as a
DeepSeek Harness bundle (`dsh-agent-relay-plugin`): DSH sessions and Codex threads
exchange messages with push delivery, thread discovery, and delegated work that
returns to the conversation that asked.

A live DSH agent (a real DSH Web session) and a persistent native Codex thread
exchange durable messages. Each side reaches the relay the way that harness is
supposed to be reached: DSH through a registered `relay_send` tool whose sender
is taken from `exec.agent`, and Codex through a member-bound stdio MCP companion
whose sender is taken from its bearer credential.

Agent Relay is a DSH bundle. Installing it adds a **disabled** Host row to a
profile; enabling that row in the profile's user layer starts the relay with every
boot of the profile.

```sh

readme.section: prebuilt tarball: no build-time scripts, no extra network
readme.text: dsh plugin --profile web add ./dsh-agent-relay-plugin-0.1.0.tgz
dsh plugin --profile web add /path/to/dsh-agent-relay

Add the enable block to `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml` (a top-level
YAML array). A later layer replaces a row's whole `config`, so repeat every key:
yaml
- id: agent-relay
  disabled: false
  config:
    codexProxy: ~/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock
    codexExecutable: /path/to/codex
    allowSessionCreation: true
    externalMembers:
      - id: codex-tui
        tokenFile: $DSH_HOME/agent-relay/codex-tui.token
```

Defaults: `teamId: relay`, `bridgePort: 33120`, journal at
`$DSH_HOME/agent-relay/journal.jsonl`, status/log beside it, and lazy attachment
to the default Codex daemon socket when no transport is configured. Restart the
profile: the relay starts with it and attaches to Codex whenever the daemon
appears, even if that is after the host booted.

Codex reaches the relay through the bundled MCP companion. Add to
`~/.codex/config.toml`, using the same token as the external member:

```toml
[mcp_servers.agent-relay]
command = "/path/to/node"
args = ["$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/node_modules/dsh-agent-relay-plugin/dist/mcp.mjs"]
default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"

Create the member token file and install the skill into both harnesses:

```sh
mkdir -p "$DSH_HOME/agent-relay" && chmod 700 "$DSH_HOME/agent-relay"
printf '%s\n' "$TOKEN" > "$DSH_HOME/agent-relay/codex-tui.token"
chmod 600 "$DSH_HOME/agent-relay/codex-tui.token"
node "$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/node_modules/dsh-agent-relay-plugin/tools/install-skill.mjs" \

Check that the layer composed without booting, then restart the profile:

```sh
dsh --profile web --dump-config | grep -A4 'id: agent-relay'
```

Uninstall: `dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-agent-relay-plugin`.

| Component | Verified against |
| --- | --- |
| DeepSeek Harness | `0.2.0-rc.2`; `engines.dsh` is `>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0` |
| Codex CLI | `0.163.0` — stdio app-server, WebSocket app-server, and the shared daemon's unix WebSocket endpoint; the protocol was first probed on `0.162.1` |
| Node | `>=22` |

Verified end to end inside a real `web` profile: push delivery in both
directions, `relay_threads` discovery, lazy attach when the Codex daemon starts
after the host, delegated work returning to the originating Codex conversation,
and the relay's own ephemeral thread staying out of the user's history. See
[Evidence](#evidence).

readme.section: How it is wired (and what stays untouched)
readme.text:
The development profile `relay-dev` is created from the shipped `web` template
inside a **separate DSH home** (`$PWD/.relay-home/dsh`), and the plugin is added
as an extra patch overlay for that boot only:

```sh

readme.section: once: create the isolated development home and profile
readme.text:
mkdir -p .relay-home/dsh
ln -s ~/.dsh/.credentials.yaml .relay-home/dsh/.credentials.yaml   # read-only reuse
DSH_HOME=$PWD/.relay-home/dsh dsh --profile relay-dev --from-default-profile web --help

DSH_HOME=$PWD/.relay-home/dsh dsh --profile relay-dev \
  --patch "$PWD/dev/relay-dev.patch.yml" --no-open --port 3099
```

The user's real `~/.dsh` profile, sessions and credentials are never modified:
the isolated home borrows the credentials file by symlink and the overlay lives
in this workspace. `cordis.patch.yml` is the same plugin as a proper bundle
layer, with its row **disabled by default** so installing the bundle alone
changes nothing until an operator enables it with a config.

readme.section: Using it with the real environment (`web-relay`)
readme.text:
A second instance runs inside the user's own `~/.dsh`, so it uses their real
credentials, models and session history. It is a **new** profile created from the
shipped web template plus a copy of their own patch layer; their `web` profile
is untouched.

```sh

readme.section: once: create the profile and mirror their bundle list + patch layer
readme.text:
DSH_HOME=~/.dsh dsh --profile web-relay --from-default-profile web --help
cp ~/.dsh/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml ~/.dsh/profiles/web-relay/cordis.patch.yml

DSH_HOME=~/.dsh dsh --profile web-relay \
  --patch "$PWD/dev/web-relay.patch.yml" --no-open --port 3100
```

Notes for that instance:

- It keeps its own journal and Codex home (`relay-personal`, `codex-personal`),
  so it never contends with the isolated `relay-dev` instance.
- It shares `~/.dsh/storages` and `~/.dsh/sessions` with any other running host
  on the same home. Two hosts are fine for reading history; keep heavy
  workspace/registry edits in one host at a time.
- `dev/web-relay.patch.yml` pins `agent-default-model` to a reachable model
  because the profile's own selection (`pai`, `127.0.0.1:30808`) was not
  reachable when it was booted. Remove that block or switch model in the GUI
  once that endpoint is up.
- Only sessions live **in that host** can be borrowed as members; sessions from
  the other host appear in its history and can be resumed there.

readme.section: Connecting a Codex you run yourself (pull path)
readme.text:
The relay drives its own managed Codex. A Codex **you** run — your TUI, your IDE
session, your daemon — is reached the other way round: it pulls.

```yaml

bridgePort: 33120                     # pin it: the member config must survive restarts
        externalMembers:
          - id: codex-tui                     # stable member identity
            token: <64 hex random string>     # operator-supplied; same value in that Codex's env
```

Then give that Codex the relay MCP server (its own `~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[mcp_servers.agent-relay]
command = "/usr/bin/node"
args = ["/path/to/dsh-agent-relay/dist/mcp.mjs"]
default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"

[mcp_servers.agent-relay.env]
AGENT_RELAY_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:33120/relay"
AGENT_RELAY_TOKEN = "<the same 64 hex token>"
```

Restart that Codex (or reload its config) and it gains `relay_send`,
`relay_inbox`, `relay_members`, `relay_status`. Semantics:

- Messages addressed to the external member stay **`queued`** — nothing is
  injected into a process the relay does not own — and they survive relay
  restarts.
- `relay_inbox` hands them over **exactly once**; the relay then records
  `accepted` with `receipt.deliveredBy: "pull"`.
- Recipients are resolved, not required verbatim: `relay_members` lists every
  member with an alias, its title and cwd (for DSH sessions), and `to` accepts an
  alias, any unique id prefix, or the full member id. Ambiguity and unknown names
  fail with the candidate list instead of guessing.
- Members can create new sessions when the operator enables it
  (`allowSessionCreation`, capped by `maxSpawnedMembers`): `relay_create_session`
  opens a fresh root DSH session in a chosen directory, or an additional
  persistent Codex thread, and can hand it its first task through the ordinary
  relay path. DSH sessions are created through the host's session controller, so
  preset and model resolve before the first turn; `dshAgentPreset` overrides the
  preset.
- The external Codex can `relay_send` to any member; the DSH side is woken
  normally.
- Push into a thread another Codex process is currently holding is

Verified end to end: `evidence/unmanaged-codex-pull.txt`, reproducible with
`node tools/unmanaged-codex-pull.mjs --url <bridge url> --token <token>`.
Copy-paste prompts for the Codex side (TUI and `codex exec`) are in
[`examples/from-codex.md`](examples/from-codex.md).

readme.section: Skill: teach the agents the protocol
readme.text:
`skills/agent-relay/` is one skill bundle both harnesses understand — a
`SKILL.md` with `name`/`description` frontmatter plus a `references/operations.md`
that is loaded only when needed. It tells an agent to find members with
`relay_members` instead of inventing ids, how to address by alias/title/prefix,
when to drain with `relay_inbox`, how requestIds make retries safe, and what each
delivery state means.

readme.section: Skill: teach the agents the protocol
readme.text:
```sh
node tools/install-skill.mjs --dry-run                  # preview
node tools/install-skill.mjs \
  --codex-home ~/.codex --dsh-home ~/.dsh --agents-home ~/.agents
```

It symlinks the repository bundle into each root, so edits here are live:

readme.section: Skill: teach the agents the protocol
readme.text:
| harness | root | discovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `$CODEX_HOME/skills/agent-relay/` | on start |
| DSH | `<dshHome>/skills/agent-relay/` (rank 400) | watched; appears without restart |
| other agents | `~/.agents/skills/agent-relay/` (DSH rank 500) | watched |

Verified on this machine: the skill is listed in a live DSH session's catalog and
in Codex's rendered prompt input (`codex debug prompt-input`).

Requires Node >= 22.

```sh
npm install
node tools/link-host-packages.mjs    # point @deepseek-ai/* at the installed DSH packages
npm run build                        # tsc -> dist/index.js, plus the runtime .mjs modules
npm test                             # 7 core/bridge/MCP tests
npm run check                        # typecheck + syntax check, no emit required

readme.section: two-round acceptance run against a booted dev host (see above)
readme.text:
node tools/round-trip.mjs
```

`tools/link-host-packages.mjs` exists because the bundle's own module lives in
this workspace: linking the `@deepseek-ai/*` dependencies to the installation
guarantees the plugin is compiled and executed against exactly the host modules
that are running, instead of a second copy from the registry.

The relay can own the Codex App Server over WebSocket instead of a private stdio
pipe. A Codex TUI then attaches to the **same conversation**, so turns the relay
pushes from DSH appear live in the session you are looking at, and turns you type
are visible to the relay.

```yaml

codexListen: ws://127.0.0.1:18799
```

The plugin spawns `codex app-server --listen <url> --ws-auth capability-token
--ws-token-file <journal>.codex-ws-token` (0600, loopback only), connects itself,
and publishes the attach command in its log and status file:sh
export AGENT_RELAY_CODEX_TOKEN=$(cat .relay-home/relay-personal/journal.jsonl.codex-ws-token)
codex --remote ws://127.0.0.1:18799 --remote-auth-token-env AGENT_RELAY_CODEX_TOKEN
```

Verified with a recording client in place of the TUI: a DSH message to `codex`
appeared as `turn/started` → `userMessage` → `mcpToolCall` → `turn/completed` in
the attached session, and Codex's reply woke the DSH session — no polling on
either side (`evidence/codex-attach-demo.txt`, `evidence/codex-ws-multiclient-probe.txt`).

Threads **you** open in that attached TUI get the relay's MCP tools too: in
WebSocket mode the plugin gives the whole app-server the MCP server at process
level, and adopts whichever thread you are in as the push member
`codex-attached` (resumed conversations included — adoption triggers on any
notification, not just `thread/started`). So `relay_members` from a DSH session
shows `codex-attached`, and messages to it run as turns in the session you are
looking at; its replies come back addressed to the sender. One attached
conversation is represented by that member at a time; opening another rebinds it.
Evidence: `evidence/codex-attached-thread-fix.txt`.
A second client can also resume the thread and submit turns; a turn submitted
while another is active merges into it, so the relay still drains only at idle
boundaries.

readme.section: Attaching the relay to a server you own (`codexAttach`)
readme.text:
The opposite split is also supported: you start the app-server (your `CODEX_HOME`,
your config, your skills) and the relay attaches as a client instead of spawning
one.

```yaml
        codexAttach: ws://127.0.0.1:18899
        codexAttachTokenFile: /path/to/that-servers-capability-token
```

```sh

readme.section: you run this, in your terminal / supervisor:
readme.text:
CODEX_HOME=~/.codex codex app-server --listen ws://127.0.0.1:18899 \
  --ws-auth capability-token --ws-token-file ~/.codex/relay-ws-token

readme.section: your TUI joins the same server (both clients see the same threads):
readme.text:
codex --remote ws://127.0.0.1:18899 --remote-auth-token-env AGENT_RELAY_CODEX_TOKEN
```

readme.section: your TUI joins the same server (both clients see the same threads):
readme.text:
The relay creates its own thread on that server and supplies the relay MCP server
through per-thread `config` (verified end to end: two-round run passed, and
stopping the relay left the external server healthy — `evidence/codex-attach-external-server.txt`).
The relay's own Codex thread on that server is **ephemeral**: it runs turns and
carries the relay MCP server, but it is not written into the user's history and
leaves no rollout (a non-ephemeral thread there would show up as an unattachable
"task" in their TUI). It is replaced on every relay start.

readme.section: your TUI joins the same server (both clients see the same threads):
readme.text:
The relay never stops a server it does not own. Two consequences:

- Threads that **other** clients create on that server get the relay tools only if
  the server itself was launched with process-level
  `-c mcp_servers.agent-relay.…` (relay-owned mode adds that automatically).
- Restarting the external server drops the relay's connection; it does not
  reconnect automatically, and deliveries around that moment are `uncertain`.

readme.section: Attaching to the daemon your TUI already uses (`codexProxy`)
readme.text:
A plain `codex` TUI joins a shared background app-server when one is running
(`codex --no-daemon` opts out), and its control socket is
`<CODEX_HOME>/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock`. The relay can join that
same daemon instead of creating its own server:

```yaml
        codexProxy: ~/.codex/app-server-control/app-server-control.sock
```

readme.section: Attaching to the daemon your TUI already uses (`codexProxy`)
readme.text:
The plugin runs `codex app-server proxy --sock <socket>` and speaks stdio JSON-RPC
through it. Consequences: the relay's thread lives in your real `~/.codex` history,
the conversation your TUI has open is discovered (via `thread/list` polling plus
notifications) and adopted as the push member — by default the first configured
external member, i.e. the identity your Codex config authenticates as — and the
daemon is never stopped on unload. Startup command (run from the terminal that
shares the daemon's `/tmp`):

readme.section: Attaching to the daemon your TUI already uses (`codexProxy`)
readme.text:
```sh
cd /path/to/dsh-agent-relay
DSH_HOME=~/.dsh dsh --profile web-relay \
  --patch "$PWD/dev/web-relay-daemon.patch.yml" --no-open --port 3102
```

readme.section: Attaching to the daemon your TUI already uses (`codexProxy`)
readme.text:
**Status: working.** The control socket is a WebSocket server at path `/`, and the
plugin talks to it directly (`UnixWebSocket` in `src/codex.mjs`) — the `ws`
library's `socketPath` option is ignored and `codex app-server proxy` did not
answer, which is what blocked earlier attempts. Verified end to end against a real
unix app-server: attach, `thread/start`, a completed turn, 23 notifications, and
the server outliving the client (`evidence/codex-shared-daemon-attach.txt`).
Start the host from the same session as the daemon:

readme.section: Attaching to the daemon your TUI already uses (`codexProxy`)
readme.text:
```sh
cd /path/to/dsh-agent-relay
DSH_HOME=~/.dsh dsh --profile web-relay \
  --patch "$PWD/dev/web-relay-daemon.patch.yml" --no-open --port 3102
```

Caveats: the proxy host must run in the same session as the daemon (its socket
lives in that session's `/tmp`); a daemon started before the current
binary/config was installed keeps that older state until restarted; and the relay
does not auto-reconnect if the daemon restarts.

For iterating on the plugin itself, install the checkout as a link so rebuilt
`dist/` files are picked up on the next host start:

```sh
npm install && npm run build
dsh plugin --profile web add /path/to/dsh-agent-relay
```

The enable block and Codex-side setup are the same as in [Install](#install).
Rebuild and restart the profile to pick up changes; `npm test` runs the full
suite and `dsh --profile web --dump-config` shows the composed layers.

readme.section: Thread discovery and addressing specific conversations
readme.text:
`relay_threads` (DSH tool and MCP tool) lists both sides: open Codex conversations
with thread ids and the member that addresses each (`codex-<8hex>`), the attached
conversation (`codex-tui`), the relay-owned thread (`codex`), and DSH sessions with
session id, title, cwd and `live`. Every persisted thread the app-server reports as
loaded becomes a push member, so a message can be written into a specific existing
Codex conversation instead of only the attached one. Ephemeral threads and threads
without a rollout are never exposed. See `evidence/thread-discovery.txt`.

Three surfaces, all usable without a Codex or DSH session:

```sh

readme.section: read-only journal (no credentials): members, messages, state counts
readme.text:
node tools/relay-cli.mjs states
node tools/relay-cli.mjs members --journal .relay-home/relay-personal/journal.jsonl
node tools/relay-cli.mjs messages --state queued --limit 20

readme.section: the bridge is loopback HTTP: every method is POST /relay with a member token
readme.text:
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:33120/relay -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"method":"members","params":{}}'

readme.section: settle mail that nobody will drain (scoped: a member can only discard its own)
readme.text:
node tools/relay-cli.mjs discard --all --reason "stale" --token "$TOKEN"
node tools/relay-cli.mjs discard <message-id> --token "$TOKEN"

readme.section: the MCP companion is stdio JSON-RPC, not HTTP: pipe frames into it
readme.text:
node tools/relay-cli.mjs mcp --token "$TOKEN" --call relay_members
printf '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}\n' | \
  AGENT_RELAY_URL=http://127.0.0.1:33120/relay AGENT_RELAY_TOKEN="$TOKEN" node dist/mcp.mjs
```

`node tools/relay-cli.mjs curl` prints all of the above with the current paths
filled in. From the Codex side, `codex mcp get agent-relay` shows how that Codex
sees the server.

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `src/index.ts` | Host plugin: borrows live DSH agents, owns the Codex thread, registers tools, compiles to `dist/index.js` |
| `src/core.mjs` | Exclusive journal owner: durable messages, request dedup, generation pinning, serialized delivery |
| `src/bridge.mjs` | Loopback HTTP API; each bearer credential binds one member generation |
| `src/codex.mjs` | Codex App Server client verified against `codex-cli 0.162.1` |
| `src/mcp.mjs` | Member-bound stdio MCP companion (`relay_send`, `relay_members`, `relay_status`) |
| `dev/relay-dev.patch.yml` | Development overlay that wires the compiled plugin into `relay-dev` |
| `cordis.patch.yml` | Bundle patch layer (row disabled until configured) |
| `tools/round-trip.mjs` | Two-round acceptance harness (creates its own DSH Web session) |
| `tools/dsh-web-client.mjs` | Token exchange + `/api` RPC client used to drive a real Web session |
| `tools/codex-mcp-approval-probe.mjs` | Probe that established which MCP approval configuration Codex accepts |
| `skills/agent-relay/` | One `SKILL.md` bundle both harnesses read: addressing, sending, draining, states |
| `tools/install-skill.mjs` | Installs that skill int

readme.section: Verified host behavior the design depends on
readme.text: DeepSeek Harness `0.2.0-rc.2` (details and quotes in `research/dsh-plugin-api.md`):

readme.section: Verified host behavior the design depends on
readme.text:
- A plugin is an ES module with `name`, `inject = ['tools', 'agents']`,
  `Config` (Schemastery) and `apply(ctx, config)`; **no** `export default`.
- `ctx.tools.register(defineTool({...}))` accepts the definition; `exec.agent`
  is the calling `Agent`, and `agent.session.id` is the live session id.
- `agent.followup(message)` queues an *ordinary next turn* and wakes the driver;
  it never steers a running step. `agent.status` (`idle`/`running`) plus the
  `agent/status` event are the idle-boundary signal.
- `ctx.agents.roots()` is how an already-open Web session is **borrowed** rather
  than recreated.
- A user-role message requires an explicit `source.kind`. The relay declares its
  own `agent-relay` kind instead of `user`, because `kind: 'user'` is the
  host-attested *human* marker that grants goal-completion authority.

readme.section: Verified host behavior the design depends on
readme.text:
- `thread/start` / `thread/resume` accept an unconstrained `config` object that
  carries per-thread MCP servers: `config.mcp_servers.<name>.{command,args,env}`.
- Threads persist across app-server restarts; `thread/resume` restores the same
  conversation (verified with a fresh process answering about an earlier turn).
- **`turn/start` is not a mutual-exclusion primitive.** A second `turn/start`
  on an active thread is accepted and its input is merged into the active turn
  instead of returning an error. The relay therefore treats `accepted` as
  "the harness admitted this input", drains only at idle boundaries, and never
  claims turn exclusivity.
- **MCP tool calls need an explicit approval mode.** With
  `approvalPolicy: 'never'`, an unconfigured MCP server fails the model's tool
  call with `MCP tool call requires approval, but approval policy is never`.
  `default_tools_approval_mode` accepts `auto | prompt | writes | approve`; only
  `approve` makes the call succeed (verified at both the `-c` and per-thread
  `config` level; `auto` and `writes` still fail). The relay sets `approve` for
  **its own MCP server only** and documents it as an operator decision.
- Server-to-clien

A send acknowledges journal persistence, not model execution. An accepted
delivery means the harness accepted the input. It does not mean consumed,
understood or done. The core records `uncertain` BEFORE submission; ambiguous
submissions are never retried automatically. Inspect native history and
reconcile it before redelivery. Already accepted messages do not replay.

Task IDs and kinds are routing metadata; there is no task scheduler or
completion engine. `kind: 'complete'` is a message from one agent, not a
verified task outcome.

Idle-boundary delivery: messages queued for a member are delivered when that
member reaches an idle boundary (Codex `turn/completed`, DSH `agent/status` →
`idle`), or immediately when a send is made. A busy DSH session receives the
callback as a queued follow-up turn, never as mid-step steering.

- **Approvals.** Codex sandbox/file-change/exec approval requests are refused,
  not routed to a DSH user surface. Until that exists, a Codex task that needs a
  sandbox approval will not complete; the refusal is recorded, and no permission
  is silently granted. `research/codex-api.md` documents the exact decision
  payloads a real approval surface must answer.
- **One process owns the journal.** A second owner is refused while the recorded
  heartbeat is fresh; a lock whose heartbeat stopped for
  `LOCK_STALE_MS` (10s) is reclaimed automatically. A torn journal still fails
  closed and needs operator repair.
- **Delivery is globally serialized** in one process, and `drain()` walks queued
  messages in order. No daemon proxy attachment, remote transport, artifact
  transfer or dashboard.
- **A recovered `uncertain` message is never retried automatically.** Reconcile
  it against native history first.
